agents.name: Oxaliplatin
agents.explanation: Oxaliplatin makes links within DNA. These interfere with copying and repair, which can stop a cancer cell dividing. Healthy tissues can also be affected.
agents.watch: Cold can trigger tingling or throat discomfort. Tell the team about persistent numbness, difficulty with buttons or walking, or infusion symptoms. New breathing difficulty always needs assessment.
risks: Persistent sensory neuropathy, sometimes lasting after treatment
Rare serious lung or blood complications

agents.name: Folinic acid
agents.explanation: Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself.
agents.watch: The combined treatment can increase mouth soreness and diarrhoea. Report these promptly. Rare allergic reactions can occur.

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.
agents.watch: Diarrhoea, mouth sores and skin soreness may become serious. Chest pain during the pump infusion needs emergency assessment. Unexpected severe early toxicity can occur even after DPD testing.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

chapters.title: Your indication and treatment aim
chapters.intro: The same medicines can have different aims.

items.title: After colon-cancer surgery
items.text: Adjuvant treatment aims to reduce recurrence risk after complete resection. The likely absolute benefit depends on stage, pathology, fitness and other features. Ask how recurrence risk and neuropathy risk influence the proposed duration.

items.title: Advanced colorectal or upper-GI cancer
items.text: Treatment may aim to control growth, relieve symptoms and prolong life. The plan is reviewed against response, toxicity and your priorities. A treatment break or a change of components requires an individual discussion.

items.title: How long will treatment last?
items.text: Do not infer duration from the number of passport pages. Ask for the planned number of cycles and review points. The NCCP schedule distinguishes adjuvant colon treatment, metastatic colorectal treatment and upper-GI treatment.

chapters.title: Living with the 46-hour pump
chapters.intro: Ask for a demonstration and written contact instructions.

items.title: Before leaving
items.text: Know what normal pump progress looks like, how to carry it and how to protect the line while washing or sleeping. Check who will disconnect it and when. Have the team check anything you do not understand.

items.title: Leakage or a delivery problem
items.text: Use the hospital spill instructions, avoid direct contact with leaked medicine and call the team. Do not repair a connection or adjust the pump. A pump finishing much sooner or later than expected also needs advice.

items.title: Chest pain while on fluorouracil
items.text: Fluorouracil can affect the heart. New chest pain during treatment needs urgent assessment; severe pain, collapse or major breathing difficulty means 112/999. Tell emergency staff that fluorouracil is infusing. Follow the team’s instructions about the pump.

chapters.title: What the checks are for
chapters.intro: Symptoms, blood results and the treatment aim answer different questions.

items.title: Blood counts
items.text: Neutrophils protect against infection, haemoglobin carries oxygen and platelets help clotting. A normal previous result or feeling well does not prove the current counts are safe. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate advice.

items.title: Kidney and liver function
items.text: Organ function can change drug exposure. Vomiting or diarrhoea can cause dehydration and worsen kidney function. Report reduced urine, poor intake, jaundice and new medicines. The clinical assessment combines results with symptoms.

items.title: Describe symptoms in practical terms
items.text: Tell the team about the worst symptoms since the last visit, even if improved today. Examples include extra stools above your usual pattern, whether mouth pain affects drinking, and whether numbness affects buttons or balance.

items.title: How benefit is assessed
items.text: After surgery, treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence; there may be no visible cancer to measure. In advanced disease, scans, symptoms and function help assess control. Ask when review is planned and what would lead to a change.

chapters.title: Recognising treatment effects
chapters.intro: Early reporting helps the team manage symptoms and protect function.

items.title: Acute cold sensitivity and persistent neuropathy
items.text: Cold-related tingling can occur soon after oxaliplatin. Persistent numbness between cycles is different and may worsen with repeated treatment. Describe duration and effect on hand use or walking. Some neuropathy can remain after treatment ends.

items.title: Bowel and mouth symptoms
items.text: Fluorouracil can affect rapidly renewing tissues. Keep track of stools compared with your normal pattern, including stoma output. Report diarrhoea, painful ulcers or reduced drinking; do not wait for the next cycle if you are dehydrated or unwell.

items.title: Hand-foot soreness and skin changes
items.text: Tell the team about red, tender or peeling palms or soles. Reduce friction and use the skin care recommended locally. Pain limiting normal activity needs review. Do not assume it must be tolerated to complete treatment.

items.title: Fatigue and nausea
items.text: Use manageable activity, rest and the prescribed anti-sickness plan. New profound weakness, faintness or breathlessness warrants assessment because anaemia, infection, dehydration and other problems can look like ordinary fatigue.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Plan around the activities and people that matter to you.

items.title: Food, drink and practical help
items.text: Use foods and drinks you can manage. Tell the team about weight loss, poor intake or difficulty shopping and cooking; ask for dietitian or practical support. A fixed daily fluid target is not appropriate for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney problems.

items.title: Activity, rest and driving
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity. Record what fatigue stops you doing. Do not drive when dizzy, unwell or affected by sedating medicines. Ask about work adjustments and transport for treatment days.

items.title: Medicines, vaccines and supplements
items.text: Bring a complete medicine list, including over-the-counter products and supplements. Ask the oncology pharmacist before changes. Discuss vaccination timing. Do not stop prescribed long-term medicines on your own.

items.title: Fertility, contraception and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment when relevant. Ask for a written contraception and breastfeeding plan covering each medicine and the period after treatment. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy.

items.title: Support for you and your family
items.text: Ask about psycho-oncology, social work, counselling and symptom support. Take information in manageable amounts. A family member or trusted person can help record questions if you wish. Discuss how treatment fits your priorities.

chapters.title: Words you may hear
chapters.intro: A short reference for clinic discussions.

items.title: Adjuvant, metastatic and cycle
items.text: Adjuvant means treatment after the main treatment, usually surgery, to reduce recurrence risk. Metastatic means spread to a distant site. A cycle includes treatment and the interval before the next planned start.

items.title: DPD, neuropathy and dose modification
items.text: DPD is an enzyme involved in fluorouracil breakdown. Neuropathy means nerve damage or dysfunction. Dose modification means changing the amount, timing or components to balance benefit and harm.

day_groups.title: Infusion and pump connection
day_groups.body: Symptoms and blood tests are reviewed. The day-ward medicines are followed by connection of a fluorouracil pump. Tell the nurse immediately about a reaction or pain at the infusion site.
day_groups.action: Before leaving, confirm the pump-care instructions, disconnection appointment and contact number.

day_groups.title: The pump is delivering treatment
day_groups.body: The infusion runs for about 46 hours from connection; the calendar day does not determine the exact finish time. Follow the instructions for keeping the line dry and secure. Avoid cold exposure if it triggers symptoms.
day_groups.action: Call for a leaking, disconnected or unexpectedly stopped pump. Do not reconnect, alter settings or disconnect it yourself unless specifically trained and instructed.

day_groups.title: After disconnection
day_groups.body: Nausea, diarrhoea, mouth symptoms, fatigue or cold sensitivity may continue. Use prescribed support. New symptoms deserve advice even if the pump has finished.
day_groups.action: Report poor intake, persistent diarrhoea or mouth pain early. Chest pain or major breathing difficulty requires emergency help.

day_groups.title: Between visits and the next review
day_groups.body: Blood counts can fall between visits. Numbness may accumulate over cycles. Describe any difficulty fastening buttons, walking or handling objects before more oxaliplatin.
day_groups.action: Bring the symptom passport and check the next appointment. Day 1 usually repeats 14 days after this cycle started, only if confirmed.

support.title: Nausea prevention and rescue
support.text: Take the prescribed prevention medicines at the planned times and keep rescue treatment available. Tell the team if nausea or constipation is not controlled; do not duplicate steroid or anti-sickness medicines.

support.title: Bowel symptoms
support.text: Report diarrhoea promptly and follow the written rescue plan. Severe symptoms, fever, dehydration or inability to drink need urgent advice.

support.title: Counts and recovery
support.text: White-cell growth-factor injections are prescribed according to individual risk and previous complications. They are not automatically required for every patient or every cycle.

support.title: Cold and nerve symptoms
support.text: Avoid cold exposure as advised after oxaliplatin. Report persistent numbness or difficulty with buttons, walking or everyday tasks before the next dose.

evidence.title: Understanding the evidence
evidence.intro: Ask which evidence matches your cancer, treatment aim and medicines.
evidence.interpretation: Adding oxaliplatin to fluorouracil-based treatment improved long-term outcomes in a study of people with stage III colon cancer after surgery. That study used FOLFOX4, a related but different schedule. It does not predict benefit for every indication of modified FOLFOX6 or for an individual person.

chronology_notes.title: Cold sensitivity

chronology_notes.title: Blood counts

chronology_notes.title: Symptoms over time

questions.q: How is my treatment chosen?
questions.a: FOLFOX-4 may be given after surgery for stage II or III colon cancer, or for colorectal cancer that has spread. Your team explains the aim, alternatives and how benefit will be reviewed.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates to understand the cycle?
questions.a: No. The graph explains a general pattern. Your hospital arranges appointments; the guide and its safety information are available without entering anything.

questions.q: Will I have a pump at home?
questions.a: Arrange Day 2 infusion renewal and final disconnection around Day 3. This is two separate 22-hour infusions; do not use a 46-hour pump timetable.

questions.q: What happens if a dose is delayed?
questions.a: The team checks the cause and may delay, reduce, change or stop one medicine. Ask which component changes and when you should next attend; do not restart yourself.

questions.q: How will I know whether it is helping?
questions.a: Scans, symptoms and clinical review assess benefit. A rash, side effect or good day alone cannot show whether the cancer is responding.

questions.q: What about radiotherapy?
questions.a: This NCCP regimen does not contain a routine radiotherapy course. If radiation is recommended separately, ask whether it is before, during or after these medicines.

questions.q: What about fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding?
questions.a: Discuss fertility preservation and reproductive plans before treatment. Ask for the contraception and breastfeeding instructions for every medicine; the whole regimen may require longer precautions than one medicine alone.

questions.q: Why is Day 2 different from other FOLFOX leaflets?
questions.a: NCCP FOLFOX-4 has fluorouracil on Days 1 and 2, each with a 22-hour infusion. It is not modified FOLFOX-6. The team confirms your Day 2 prescription and visit; do not rely on another FOLFOX schedule.

patient.phases_note: This is a general explanation, not an appointment calendar. Delays or changes are decided by your team. Each medicine can need a different change.
patient.timeline_note: NCCP defines the treatment days. Symptom bands are broad educational guidance; reactions can occur on any day, and cumulative effects may continue between cycles.
patient.safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell require immediate contact. Serious symptoms override any timeline or diary.
patient.teachback: Can you explain which visits are planned, whether a pump is involved, and which symptoms mean you should call today? No dates or symptom scores are needed to use this guide.
patient.consent_support: Discuss the treatment aim, alternatives, expected benefit, serious and lasting risks, fertility/pregnancy precautions and the contact plan. Explain DPD testing and the exact pump schedule.
patient.urgent_extra: New breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse, severe diarrhoea or inability to drink require prompt assessment. Call for line pain, swelling, leakage or unexpected pump progress.

clinical.component_rationale: Oxaliplatin makes links within DNA. These interfere with copying and repair, which can stop a cancer cell dividing. Healthy tissues can also be affected. Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself. Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.

items.title: Why this treatment?
items.text: Capecitabine is chemotherapy taken as tablets. NCCP 00216 covers several colorectal and breast cancer settings, including treatment after surgery and treatment of advanced disease. Ask which aim and duration apply to you.

items.title: How long?
items.text: NCCP recommends six months / eight cycles for adjuvant colon or residual triple-negative breast cancer. For advanced disease, duration depends on response and tolerability.

items.title: Alternatives and decisions
items.text: Discuss the expected benefit, burdens, reasonable alternatives and the option of supportive care. The best choice depends on your cancer, fitness and preferences.

chapters.title: Taking capecitabine safely
chapters.intro: Tablets are active chemotherapy, with a specific schedule.

items.title: Meals and doses
items.text: Use your current prescription. Swallow tablets whole with water with or within 30 minutes after food. Do not cut, chew or crush them; ask pharmacy if swallowing is difficult.

items.title: Missed doses or vomiting
items.text: Do not replace a missed or vomited dose. Never double the next dose. Contact the team for repeated vomiting or uncertainty about the schedule.

items.title: Pause and restart
items.text: Stop tablets for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth/hand-foot symptoms affecting activity, fever or dehydration and seek advice. A toxicity-related pause requires instructions before restart.

items.title: Different tablet strengths
items.text: Different strengths may be combined to make your dose. A reduction changes tablet numbers: use the new label and do not calculate a change from this page.

chapters.title: Tests and checks
chapters.intro: Monitoring helps the team decide whether treatment can continue.

items.title: DPD testing
items.text: DPD helps break down fluoropyrimidine medicines. Low activity can cause severe toxicity; testing before treatment helps guide the plan but cannot prevent every serious reaction.

items.title: Blood, kidney and liver results
items.text: Counts, kidney and liver function are checked before each cycle. Diarrhoea and poor intake can worsen kidney function and make tablets harder to tolerate.

items.title: Your symptoms matter
items.text: Report bowel frequency, stoma output, mouth soreness, hand-foot pain, chest symptoms and what daily activities you can no longer manage.

items.title: Additional checks
items.text: The team sets the scan or follow-up plan for your particular treatment aim.

chapters.title: Recognise symptoms and act
chapters.intro: Do not wait for the next appointment if you feel unwell.

items.title: Bowel and hydration
items.text: Report diarrhoea or increased stoma output early. Inability to drink, dizziness, very little urine, severe pain or blood in stool needs prompt assessment.

items.title: Hands, feet and mouth
items.text: Pain, cracking, peeling or ulcers that affect normal activities or eating/drinking need advice. Gentle preventive care helps, but does not replace reporting.

items.title: Chest symptoms and infection
items.text: Stop capecitabine and seek urgent assessment for chest pain. Fever, shaking chills or sudden illness needs immediate oncology contact, even if the temperature is normal.

items.title: Treatment-specific effects
items.text: Severe toxicity can happen early. Do not assume that tablets are mild treatment or that a normal DPD result makes symptoms safe to ignore.

chapters.title: Daily life and other medicines
chapters.intro: Make the plan fit your practical needs.

items.title: Eating, drinking and activity
items.text: Aim for tolerable meals and fluids; contact the team if intake falls. Gentle activity and rest can be adjusted to your energy. Ask for dietetic help if needed.

items.title: Medicine and supplement checks
items.text: Check new medicines with oncology pharmacy. Warfarin can require closer INR checks; phenytoin levels may need monitoring. Brivudine is an important prohibited interaction.

items.title: Family, work and fertility
items.text: Ask about infection exposure, work, intimacy, contraception, fertility and any caring responsibilities. Use the medicine-specific duration of precautions given by your team.

items.title: Procedures and travel
items.text: Plan transport and support around appointments. Ask which symptoms or blood-count problems affect travel and when to contact the service.

questions.q: What is the aim of my treatment?
questions.a: Capecitabine is chemotherapy taken as tablets. NCCP 00216 covers several colorectal and breast cancer settings, including treatment after surgery and treatment of advanced disease. Ask which aim and duration apply to you.

questions.q: Which days do I take the tablets?
questions.a: capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14, then no capecitabine on Days 15–21. Follow your individual prescription.

questions.q: What if I forget a dose or vomit?
questions.a: Do not take an extra dose. Take the next planned dose at its usual time unless treatment has been stopped; report repeated vomiting and check with the team if unsure.

questions.q: When should I stop tablets and call?
questions.a: Stop capecitabine and contact oncology for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth or hand-foot symptoms affecting activity, vomiting that prevents drinking, fever or sudden illness. Do not restart after a toxicity interruption until the team advises.

questions.q: Why do I need blood tests if I take tablets at home?

agents.name: Irinotecan
agents.explanation: The body converts irinotecan into SN-38. This traps an enzyme called topoisomerase I while DNA is being copied, causing damage that can stop cancer cells dividing. Normal bowel and blood-forming cells can also be affected.
agents.watch: Tell the nurse immediately about cramps, sweating or diarrhoea during the infusion. Diarrhoea starting later needs the separate written treatment and contact plan.
risks: Rare serious lung or allergic reactions

agents.name: Folinic acid
agents.explanation: Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself.
agents.watch: The combined treatment can increase mouth soreness and diarrhoea. Report these promptly. Rare allergic reactions can occur.

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.
agents.watch: Diarrhoea, mouth sores and skin soreness may become serious. Chest pain during the pump infusion needs emergency assessment. Unexpected severe early toxicity can occur even after DPD testing.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Will I need a port or a PICC?
questions.a: The team chooses the most suitable access device with you. A port is under the skin; a PICC enters through the upper arm and has an external section. Both require specific care, and the pump can be used with either.

questions.q: Does disconnecting the pump remove my port?
questions.a: No. At the arranged visit the pump is disconnected and the line cared for. A port needle may be removed, but the implanted port stays under the skin until a separate removal procedure is arranged.

questions.q: What if the pump finishes early or still looks full?
questions.a: Contact the team for advice. Do not change delivery settings or disconnect or reconnect it yourself. Follow only the specific emergency steps you have been taught.

questions.q: Is delayed diarrhoea the same as cramps during infusion?
questions.a: No. Irinotecan can cause an early reaction with cramps, sweating or diarrhoea, and a later diarrhoea problem. Tell the nurse about early symptoms and follow the separate written plan at home.

items.text: FOLFIRI combines irinotecan, folinic acid and fluorouracil. NCCP 00227 covers advanced colorectal cancer, metastatic oesophageal cancer and second-line advanced pancreatic cancer. Your team confirms your indication and treatment aim.

items.text: Ask when scans and clinical review will assess benefit. Treatment may be adjusted if it is not helping or side effects outweigh benefit. A cycle delay is not itself proof that treatment has stopped working.

items.title: Your priorities matter
items.text: Discuss symptoms you want to improve, daily activities, work, caring responsibilities and time at home. The team can explain alternatives and how they compare in your situation.

chapters.title: Bowel symptoms: act early
chapters.intro: Keep the written plan with your medicines.

items.title: During the infusion
items.text: With irinotecan, sudden cramps, sweating, a runny nose or diarrhoea can occur during or soon after treatment. Tell the nurse immediately; this needs a different approach from delayed diarrhoea.

items.title: At home
items.text: Record changes from your usual bowel pattern or stoma output. Follow your prescribed diarrhoea plan and contact oncology if symptoms persist or you cannot replace lost fluids. Do not wait for the next scheduled visit.

items.title: Get urgent advice
items.text: Fever, severe pain, blood in stools, dizziness, reduced urine or inability to drink alongside diarrhoea needs urgent assessment. Severe abdominal pain must not be assumed to be an ordinary treatment effect.

chapters.title: Tests and preparation
chapters.intro: Checks support safe treatment even when you feel well.

items.title: Blood tests and symptoms
items.text: The team reviews blood counts, kidney and liver function and symptoms before another cycle. Missing information is not assumed to be normal.

items.title: DPD and fluorouracil
items.text: DPD helps the body break down fluorouracil. Deficiency can cause severe toxicity. Testing guides the plan but cannot exclude all serious reactions; unexpectedly severe early diarrhoea, mouth sores or illness needs immediate review.

items.title: Additional checks
items.text: Tell the team about liver disease, previous severe diarrhoea, heart problems and all medicines. Irinotecan handling can differ between people; any additional testing is decided by your team.

chapters.title: Eating, activity and daily life
chapters.intro: Choose manageable steps and ask for help early.

items.title: Food and fluids
items.text: Take prescribed anti-sickness medicines. Small regular meals may be easier when appetite is low. Tell the team if vomiting, mouth soreness or diarrhoea prevents enough intake; follow any fluid restriction you have.

items.title: Activity and rest
items.text: Short, comfortable activity and planned rests can help you organise the day. Avoid activity that pulls the line or risks damaging the pump. Ask about work, driving and travel around your own treatment and symptoms.

items.title: Sex, fertility and pregnancy
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment where relevant. Ask about contraception, pregnancy, breastfeeding and precautions around sex during treatment; the required precautions depend on the medicines.

chapters.title: Medicines and supportive care
chapters.intro: Bring a complete list, including supplements.

items.title: Before adding medicines
items.text: Check new prescriptions, over-the-counter products and supplements with the oncology pharmacist. Do not independently stop regular medicines such as anticoagulants before a procedure.

items.title: Supportive prescriptions
items.text: Keep anti-sickness medicines and the bowel-symptom plan accessible. If growth-factor injections are prescribed, confirm when they are due in relation to the pump; do not infer timing from the graph.

items.title: Treatment changes
items.text: Ask which medicine is being delayed, reduced or stopped and why. Each medicine can change separately; record the agreed plan in your own treatment documents.

chapters.title: Prepare for the next conversation
chapters.intro: You do not have to remember everything.

items.title: Bring your questions
items.text: Use the passport to note symptoms and their effect on eating, drinking, sleep and everyday tasks. You do not need to work out which medicine caused them.

items.title: Ask for practical support
items.text: Ask for a written appointment and contact plan, an interpreter if needed, and help for a family member or carer learning the pump instructions.

items.title: Tell us what was unclear
items.text: Ask the nurse to demonstrate the pump and line, then explain back when and how you would seek help. More explanation is appropriate whenever you need it.

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

chapters.title: Treatment aim and duration
chapters.intro: CAPOX is used in several distinct settings.

items.title: Adjuvant colon cancer
items.text: Following resection of stage III colon cancer, CAPOX aims to reduce recurrence risk. Duration is a discussion about cancer risk and toxicity; three and six months are not interchangeable for everyone.

items.title: Advanced colorectal cancer
items.text: The aim may be cancer control, symptom relief and longer survival. Molecular findings, previous therapy and fitness affect the overall plan. Additional targeted medicines require their own regimen and counselling.

items.title: After gastric surgery
items.text: The adjuvant gastric evidence concerns a specific postoperative setting after D2 gastrectomy. Nutrition, postoperative recovery and oral tolerance need particular attention.

items.title: Alternatives and review points
items.text: Ask why this oral/infusion combination was chosen, whether an infusional alternative is suitable, and what would prompt a pause or change. Taking tablets at home does not mean the treatment is mild.

chapters.title: Taking capecitabine safely
chapters.intro: Your prescription is the authority for dose and dates.

items.title: Food, doses and tablet handling
items.text: Take doses about 12 hours apart and within 30 minutes after food, as instructed. Swallow whole with water. If swallowing is difficult, ask the oncology pharmacist for a safe plan. Do not crush tablets or improvise a liquid.

items.title: Missed or vomited doses
items.text: Do not replace a missed or vomited dose and do not take an extra dose. Record it and resume the next scheduled dose only if otherwise safe under your written instructions. Repeated vomiting or uncertainty needs a call.

items.title: When to stop and call
items.text: Do not continue through significant diarrhoea, painful mouth sores, painful hand-foot symptoms, fever, dehydration or chest pain. Stop capecitabine and obtain prompt advice. A clinician decides whether and how to restart.

items.title: The rest week is part of treatment
items.text: Days without tablets are planned. Do not fill them with leftovers. Return unused medicine through the hospital/pharmacy process and keep it out of household waste and away from other people.

chapters.title: What the checks are for
chapters.intro: Symptoms, blood results and the treatment aim answer different questions.

items.title: Blood counts
items.text: Neutrophils protect against infection, haemoglobin carries oxygen and platelets help clotting. A normal previous result or feeling well does not prove the current counts are safe. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate advice.

items.title: Kidney and liver function
items.text: Organ function can change drug exposure. Vomiting or diarrhoea can cause dehydration and worsen kidney function. Report reduced urine, poor intake, jaundice and new medicines. The clinical assessment combines results with symptoms.

items.title: Describe symptoms in practical terms
items.text: Tell the team about the worst symptoms since the last visit, even if improved today. Examples include extra stools above your usual pattern, whether mouth pain affects drinking, and whether numbness affects buttons or balance.

items.title: How benefit is assessed
items.text: After surgery, treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence; there may be no visible cancer to measure. In advanced disease, scans, symptoms and function help assess control. Ask when review is planned and what would lead to a change.

chapters.title: Separate the symptoms from the cause
chapters.intro: You do not need to diagnose an adverse effect before calling.

items.title: Hand-foot syndrome versus neuropathy
items.text: Capecitabine can cause tender, red or peeling palms and soles. Oxaliplatin more often causes cold-triggered tingling and cumulative numbness. Both can affect walking or hand use. Tell the team about both the sensation and what you can no longer do.

items.title: Diarrhoea and dehydration
items.text: Record stools above your own usual pattern, night-time symptoms and stoma output if relevant. Reduced urine, dizziness, inability to drink or worsening diarrhoea needs prompt advice. A medicine to stop diarrhoea does not replace the interruption plan.

items.title: Mouth, appetite and fatigue
items.text: Mouth soreness can make food and fluid difficult. Start gentle mouth care and report painful swallowing or reduced intake. Ask for symptom and nutritional support. New major weakness or breathlessness needs assessment.

items.title: Heart or infusion symptoms
items.text: Fluoropyrimidines can cause serious cardiac effects; oxaliplatin can cause allergic reactions. New chest symptoms, fainting or breathing difficulty need urgent assessment. Do not assume these are anxiety or ordinary cold sensitivity.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Plan around the activities and people that matter to you.

items.title: Food, drink and practical help
items.text: Use foods and drinks you can manage. Tell the team about weight loss, poor intake or difficulty shopping and cooking; ask for dietitian or practical support. A fixed daily fluid target is not appropriate for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney problems.

items.title: Activity, rest and driving
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity. Record what fatigue stops you doing. Do not drive when dizzy, unwell or affected by sedating medicines. Ask about work adjustments and transport for treatment days.

items.title: Medicines, vaccines and supplements
items.text: Bring a complete medicine list, including over-the-counter products and supplements. Ask the oncology pharmacist before changes. Discuss vaccination timing. Do not stop prescribed long-term medicines on your own.

items.title: Fertility, contraception and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment when relevant. Ask for a written contraception and breastfeeding plan covering each medicine and the period after treatment. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy.

items.title: Support for you and your family
items.text: Ask about psycho-oncology, social work, counselling and symptom support. Take information in manageable amounts. A family member or trusted person can help record questions if you wish. Discuss how treatment fits your priorities.

items.title: Adherence and interruption
items.text: Adherence means following the agreed plan, including stopping for toxicity when instructed. Interrupting tablets and calling about a serious symptom is part of safe treatment, not a failure to comply.

chronology_notes.title: Hands, feet and bowel

chronology_notes.title: Blood counts

chronology_notes.title: Cold and nerve symptoms

agents.name: Bevacizumab
agents.explanation: Bevacizumab binds VEGF, a signal that helps blood vessels grow. Blocking it can restrict the blood supply supporting a tumour. It also affects normal blood vessels and healing, which is why blood pressure, urine and planned procedures matter.
agents.watch: Report bleeding, a wound that is not healing, severe abdominal pain, new swelling, chest symptoms or a severe headache. Tell the team before surgery, dental procedures or port insertion.

agents.name: Oxaliplatin
agents.explanation: Oxaliplatin makes links within DNA. These interfere with copying and repair, which can stop a cancer cell dividing. Healthy tissues can also be affected.
agents.watch: Cold can trigger tingling or throat discomfort. Tell the team about persistent numbness, difficulty with buttons or walking, or infusion symptoms. New breathing difficulty always needs assessment.
risks: Persistent sensory neuropathy, sometimes lasting after treatment
Rare serious lung or blood complications

agents.name: Folinic acid
agents.explanation: Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself.
agents.watch: The combined treatment can increase mouth soreness and diarrhoea. Report these promptly. Rare allergic reactions can occur.

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.
agents.watch: Diarrhoea, mouth sores and skin soreness may become serious. Chest pain during the pump infusion needs emergency assessment. Unexpected severe early toxicity can occur even after DPD testing.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Will I need a port or a PICC?
questions.a: The team chooses the most suitable access device with you. A port is under the skin; a PICC enters through the upper arm and has an external section. Both require specific care, and the pump can be used with either.

questions.q: Does disconnecting the pump remove my port?
questions.a: No. At the arranged visit the pump is disconnected and the line cared for. A port needle may be removed, but the implanted port stays under the skin until a separate removal procedure is arranged.

questions.q: What if the pump finishes early or still looks full?
questions.a: Contact the team for advice. Do not change delivery settings or disconnect or reconnect it yourself. Follow only the specific emergency steps you have been taught.

items.title: DPD and fluorouracil
items.text: DPD helps the body break down fluorouracil. Deficiency can cause severe toxicity. Testing guides the plan but cannot exclude all serious reactions; unexpectedly severe early diarrhoea, mouth sores or illness needs immediate review.

items.text: Bevacizumab requires blood-pressure and urine-protein checks. Report any wound, bleeding, clot history or planned procedure.

items.text: Short, comfortable activity and planned rests can help you organise the day. Avoid activity that pulls the line or risks damaging the pump. Ask about work, driving and travel around your own treatment and symptoms.

items.title: Sex, fertility and pregnancy

agents.name: Bevacizumab
agents.explanation: Bevacizumab binds VEGF, a signal that helps blood vessels grow. Blocking it can restrict the blood supply supporting a tumour. It also affects normal blood vessels and healing, which is why blood pressure, urine and planned procedures matter.
agents.watch: Report bleeding, a wound that is not healing, severe abdominal pain, new swelling, chest symptoms or a severe headache. Tell the team before surgery, dental procedures or port insertion.

agents.name: Irinotecan
agents.explanation: The body converts irinotecan into SN-38. This traps an enzyme called topoisomerase I while DNA is being copied, causing damage that can stop cancer cells dividing. Normal bowel and blood-forming cells can also be affected.
agents.watch: Tell the nurse immediately about cramps, sweating or diarrhoea during the infusion. Diarrhoea starting later needs the separate written treatment and contact plan.
risks: Rare serious lung or allergic reactions

agents.name: Folinic acid
agents.explanation: Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself.
agents.watch: The combined treatment can increase mouth soreness and diarrhoea. Report these promptly. Rare allergic reactions can occur.

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.
agents.watch: Diarrhoea, mouth sores and skin soreness may become serious. Chest pain during the pump infusion needs emergency assessment. Unexpected severe early toxicity can occur even after DPD testing.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Will I need a port or a PICC?
questions.a: The team chooses the most suitable access device with you. A port is under the skin; a PICC enters through the upper arm and has an external section. Both require specific care, and the pump can be used with either.

questions.q: Does disconnecting the pump remove my port?
questions.a: No. At the arranged visit the pump is disconnected and the line cared for. A port needle may be removed, but the implanted port stays under the skin until a separate removal procedure is arranged.

questions.q: What if the pump finishes early or still looks full?
questions.a: Contact the team for advice. Do not change delivery settings or disconnect or reconnect it yourself. Follow only the specific emergency steps you have been taught.

questions.q: Is delayed diarrhoea the same as cramps during infusion?
questions.a: No. Irinotecan can cause an early reaction with cramps, sweating or diarrhoea, and a later diarrhoea problem. Tell the nurse about early symptoms and follow the separate written plan at home.

items.text: With irinotecan, sudden cramps, sweating, a runny nose or diarrhoea can occur during or soon after treatment. Tell the nurse immediately; this needs a different approach from delayed diarrhoea.

items.text: Record changes from your usual bowel pattern or stoma output. Follow your prescribed diarrhoea plan and contact oncology if symptoms persist or you cannot replace lost fluids. Do not wait for the next scheduled visit.

items.title: Blood tests and symptoms

items.title: DPD and fluorouracil
items.text: DPD helps the body break down fluorouracil. Deficiency can cause severe toxicity. Testing guides the plan but cannot exclude all serious reactions; unexpectedly severe early diarrhoea, mouth sores or illness needs immediate review.

items.title: Additional checks
items.text: Bevacizumab requires blood-pressure and urine-protein checks. Report any wound, bleeding, clot history or planned procedure.

items.title: Food and fluids
items.text: Take prescribed anti-sickness medicines. Small regular meals may be easier when appetite is low. Tell the team if vomiting, mouth soreness or diarrhoea prevents enough intake; follow any fluid restriction you have.

items.title: Activity and rest
items.text: Short, comfortable activity and planned rests can help you organise the day. Avoid activity that pulls the line or risks damaging the pump. Ask about work, driving and travel around your own treatment and symptoms.

items.title: Sex, fertility and pregnancy
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment where relevant. Ask about contraception, pregnancy, breastfeeding and precautions around sex during treatment; the required precautions depend on the medicines.

sections.text: Use the prescribed morning and evening dose within 30 minutes after food on the agreed treatment days. Do not make up a missed or vomited dose. Follow the team’s hold instructions for significant diarrhoea, mouth soreness or painful hands and feet, and contact them promptly.

chapters.title: Taking capecitabine safely
chapters.intro: Tablets are active chemotherapy, with a specific schedule.

items.title: Meals and doses
items.text: Use your current prescription. Swallow tablets whole with water with or within 30 minutes after food. Do not cut, chew or crush them; ask pharmacy if swallowing is difficult.

items.title: Missed doses or vomiting
items.text: Do not replace a missed or vomited dose. Never double the next dose. Contact the team for repeated vomiting or uncertainty about the schedule.

items.title: Pause and restart
items.text: Stop tablets for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth/hand-foot symptoms affecting activity, fever or dehydration and seek advice. A toxicity-related pause requires instructions before restart.

items.title: Different tablet strengths
items.text: Different strengths may be combined to make your dose. A reduction changes tablet numbers: use the new label and do not calculate a change from this page.

chapters.title: Tests and checks
chapters.intro: Monitoring helps the team decide whether treatment can continue.

items.title: DPD testing
items.text: DPD helps break down fluoropyrimidine medicines. Low activity can cause severe toxicity; testing before treatment helps guide the plan but cannot prevent every serious reaction.

items.title: Blood, kidney and liver results
items.text: Counts, kidney and liver function are checked before each cycle. Diarrhoea and poor intake can worsen kidney function and make tablets harder to tolerate.

items.title: Your symptoms matter
items.text: Report bowel frequency, stoma output, mouth soreness, hand-foot pain, chest symptoms and what daily activities you can no longer manage.

items.title: Additional checks
items.text: Blood pressure, urine protein, bleeding/clot symptoms and healing of wounds are checked with bevacizumab.

chapters.title: Recognise symptoms and act
chapters.intro: Do not wait for the next appointment if you feel unwell.

items.title: Bowel and hydration
items.text: Report diarrhoea or increased stoma output early. Inability to drink, dizziness, very little urine, severe pain or blood in stool needs prompt assessment.

items.title: Hands, feet and mouth
items.text: Pain, cracking, peeling or ulcers that affect normal activities or eating/drinking need advice. Gentle preventive care helps, but does not replace reporting.

items.title: Chest symptoms and infection
items.text: Stop capecitabine and seek urgent assessment for chest pain. Fever, shaking chills or sudden illness needs immediate oncology contact, even if the temperature is normal.

items.title: Treatment-specific effects
items.text: Bevacizumab can cause high blood pressure, urine protein, bleeding, clotting and healing problems. Report severe unusual headache, weakness, significant bleeding or severe abdominal pain urgently.

chapters.title: Daily life and other medicines
chapters.intro: Make the plan fit your practical needs.

items.title: Eating, drinking and activity
items.text: Aim for tolerable meals and fluids; contact the team if intake falls. Gentle activity and rest can be adjusted to your energy. Ask for dietetic help if needed.

items.title: Medicine and supplement checks
items.text: Check new medicines with oncology pharmacy. Warfarin can require closer INR checks; phenytoin levels may need monitoring. Brivudine is an important prohibited interaction.

items.title: Family, work and fertility
items.text: Ask about infection exposure, work, intimacy, contraception, fertility and any caring responsibilities. Use the medicine-specific duration of precautions given by your team.

items.title: Procedures and travel
items.text: Tell the team about planned procedures and travel. With bevacizumab, the timing of surgery and wound healing affects treatment scheduling; never arrange a dose pause yourself.

chapters.title: Review, recovery and follow-up
chapters.intro: Your plan can change as treatment progresses.

items.title: Dose changes are individual
items.text: A pause or reduction may be needed because of symptoms, blood results or kidney function. The team considers the treatment aim and other options.

items.title: After the last dose
items.text: Keep reporting new or persistent symptoms after treatment ends. Your team confirms follow-up, scans and recovery support; the timeline is not a forecast.

items.title: Prepare for review
items.text: Bring questions, symptoms and missed-dose records. Tell the team what matters most to you and ask them to explain the next decision.

questions.q: What is the aim of my treatment?
questions.a: This combination treats metastatic or unresectable colorectal cancer when an irinotecan- or oxaliplatin-based combination is unsuitable. Its aims may include cancer control, symptom relief and longer survival.

questions.q: Which days do I take the tablets?
questions.a: Bevacizumab infusion on Day 1; capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14, then no capecitabine on Days 15–21. Follow your individual prescription.

questions.q: What if I forget a dose or vomit?
questions.a: Do not take an extra dose. Take the next planned dose at its usual time unless treatment has been stopped; report repeated vomiting and check with the team if unsure.

questions.q: When should I stop tablets and call?
questions.a: Stop capecitabine and contact oncology for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth or hand-foot symptoms affecting activity, vomiting that prevents drinking, fever or sudden illness. Do not restart after a toxicity interruption until the team advises. Severe abdominal pain, significant bleeding, sudden weakness or a severe unusual headache also need urgent assessment.

questions.q: Why do I need blood tests if I take tablets at home?
questions.a: Blood counts, kidney and liver results, together with symptoms, guide whether to continue and at what dose.

questions.q: Do I need a port or a pump?
questions.a: No take-home chemotherapy pump is used. Bevacizumab needs an IV infusion; your team chooses a cannula or suitable existing line.

questions.q: What happens after treatment?
questions.a: Ask for your review and follow-up plan. Continue reporting symptoms after the last dose; further therapy depends on the treatment aim and response.
